edition.locus: Divine Institutes 6.15 (adfectus naturales / uirtus in uitiis / Stoici nomina)
edition.license: Public domain / CSEL TEI as applicable

source_text: Haec enim naturalia esse, non uoluntaria, omnium uiuentium ratio demonstrat, quae isdem omnibus quatitur adfectibus. Peripatetici ergo rectius, qui haec omnia detrahi negant posse, quia nobiscum simul nata sint, et conantur ostendere quam prouidenter et quam necessario deus siue natura — sic enim dicunt — his nos armarit adfectibus: quos tamen, quia uitiosi plerumque fiunt, si nimii sint, posse ab homine adhibito modo salubriter temperari, ut tantum homini quantum naturae satis est relinquatur. non insipiens disputatio, si, ut dixi, non ad hanc uitam omnia referrentur. Stoici ergo furiosi, qui ea non temperant, sed abscidunt rebusque natura insitis castrare hominem quodammodo uolunt. quod tale est, quale si uelint aut metum detrahere ceruis aut uenenum anguibus aut iram feris aut placiditatem pecudibus. nam quae singula mutis animalibus data sunt, ea uero uniuersa homini simul. quodsi, ut medici adfirmant, laetitiae adfectus in splene est, irae in felle, libidinis in iecore, timoris in corde, facilius est interficere animal ipsum quam ex corpore aliquid euellere: quod est animantis naturam uelle mutare. sed homines prudentes non intellegunt, cum uitia ex homine tollunt, etiam uirtutem se tollere, cui soli locum faciunt. nam si uirtus est in medio irae inpetu se ipsum cohibere ac reprimere, quod negare non possunt, caret ergo uirtute quisque ira caret. si uirtus est libidinem corporis continere, uirtute careat necesse est qui libidinem quam temperet non habet. si uirtus est cupiditatem ab alieni adpetitione frenare, nullam certe uirtutem potest habere qui caret eo ad quod cohibendum uirtutis usus adhibetur. ubi ergo uitia non sunt, ne uirtuti quidem locus est, sicut ne uictoriae quidem, ubi aduersarius nullus est. ita fit ut bonum sine malo esse in hac uita non possit. adfectus igitur quasi ubertas est naturalis animorum. nam sicut in senes ager qui est natura fecundus exuberat, sic animus incultus uitiis sua sponte inualescentibus uelut spinis obducitur. sed cum uerus cultor accesserit, statim cedentibus uitiis fruges uirtutis oriuntur. deus itaque cum hominem primum fingeret, mirabili prouidentia ingenerauit ei prius istas animi commotiones, ut posset capere uirtutem sicut terra culturam, posuitque materiam uitiorum in adfectibus, uirtutis in uitiis. quae profecto aut nulla erit aut in usu esse non poterit, si desint ea per quae uis eius aut apparet aut constat. uideamus nunc, idem illi qui uitia penitus excidunt quid effecerint. quattuor illos adfectus, quos ex opinione bonorum malorumque nasci putant, quibus euulsis sanandum esse animum sapientis existimant, quoniam intellegunt et natura insitos esse et sine iis nihil moneri, nihil agi posse, alia quaedam in eorum locum uicemque subponunt. pro cupiditate substituunt uoluntatem, quasi uero non multo sit praestabilius bonum cupere quam [malum] uelle; item pro laetitia gaudium, pro metu cautionem. at in illo quarto inmutandi nominis eos ratio deficit. itaque aegritudinem penitus id est maestitiam doloremque animi sustulerunt: quod fieri nequaquam potest. quis enim possit non dolere, si patriam aut pestilentia exhauserit aut hostis euerterit aut tyrannus oppresserit? potest aliquis non dolere, si sublatam uiderit libertatem, si proximos, si amicos, si bonos uiros aut exterminatos aut crudelissime trucidatos? nisi cuius mens ita obstipuerit, ut sit ei sensus omnis ereptus. quare aut omnia tollere debuerunt aut inplenda fuerat curta haec ac debilis disputatio, id est etiam pro aegritudine aliquid reponendum, quoniam superioribus ita ordinatis hoc consequens erat. ut enim praesentibus laetamur bonis, sic malis angimur ac dolemus. si ergo laetitiae, quoniam uitiosam putabant, nomen aliut indiderunt, sic aegritudini, quoniam et ipsam uitiosam putant, aliut uocabulum tribui congruebat. unde apparet non illis rem defuisse, sed uerbum: cuius indigentia eum totum adfectum qui est uel maximus, contra quam natura pateretur auferre uoluerunt. nam illas nominum commutationes poteram coarguere pluribus et ostendere aut sermonis ornandi augendaeque copiae gratia multa nomina isdem rebus inposita aut certe non multum inter se illa distare. nam et cupiditas a uoluntate incipit et cautio a metu oritur et laetitia nihil aliut est quam professum gaudium. sed putemus, ut ipsi uolunt, esse diuersa. nempe igitur cupiditatem esse dicent perseuerantem ac perpetuam uoluntatem, laetitiam uero insolenter se efferens gaudium, metum autem nimiam et excedentem modum cautionem. ita fit ut ea quae tollenda esse censent non tollant, sed temperent, siquidem nomina tantummodo immutant, res ipsae manent. eo igitur inprudentes reuoluuntur quo Peripatetici ratione perueniunt, ut uitia quoniam tolli non possunt, medie temperanda sint. errant ergo, quia non efficiunt quod uolunt, et longo asperoque circuitu in eandem uiam redeunt.
pass_a_gloss: Affections are natural, not voluntary — every living thing is shaken by them. Peripatetics are nearer the mark: they cannot be torn out because born with us; God (or nature) armed us with them, and excess can be tempered. Stoics are mad to cut them off — like stripping deer of fear or snakes of venom. Joy, anger, lust, fear sit in the body's organs; easier to kill the animal than rip them out. Cut vices and you cut virtue: virtue is restraining anger, containing lust, bridling greed — without the matter, no victory. Affections are the mind's natural richness: uncultivated they grow thorns; the true cultivator brings virtue's crop. God sowed motions of mind so we could take virtue as earth takes tillage — matter of vices in affections, of virtue in vices. Stoics rename desire will, joy gladness, fear caution, and try to abolish grief — which nature forbids when homeland or friends perish. They only change names; things remain. So they circle back to Peripatetic tempering — and still miss the mark.
pass_b_english: For that these are natural, not voluntary, the account of all living things shows, which is shaken by the same affections in all. The Peripatetics therefore more rightly deny that all these can be taken away, because they were born together with us, and they try to show how providently and how necessarily God or nature — for so they say — armed us with these affections: which nevertheless, because they often become vicious if they are excessive, can be temperately moderated by a human with measure applied, so that only so much is left to the human as is enough for nature. Not a foolish dispute, if, as I said, they did not refer everything to this life. The Stoics therefore are mad, who do not temper these things but cut them off and wish somehow to castrate the human of things planted by nature. Which is such as if they wished either to take fear from deer or venom from snakes or anger from wild beasts or mildness from cattle. For what were given one by one to mute animals were truly given all at once to the human. But if, as physicians affirm, the affection of joy is in the spleen, of anger in the gall, of lust in the liver, of fear in the heart, it is easier to kill the animal itself than to tear something out of the body: which is to wish to change the nature of a living thing.

But prudent humans do not understand that when they take vices from the human they also take virtue, for which alone they make a place. For if virtue is to restrain and check oneself in the midst of anger's rush — which they cannot deny — then whoever lacks anger lacks virtue. If virtue is to contain the body's lust, he must lack virtue who does not have lust to temper. If virtue is to bridle desire from seeking another's goods, he can certainly have no virtue who lacks that toward whose restraining the use of virtue is applied. Where therefore there are no vices, there is not even a place for virtue, just as not even for victory where there is no adversary. So it happens that good cannot be without evil in this life. Affections therefore are as it were the natural richness of minds. For as a field which is fertile by nature overflows in old age, so an uncultivated mind is covered with vices growing strong of their own accord as with thorns. But when the true cultivator has come, at once with vices yielding the crops of virtue arise. God therefore, when he first formed the human, by marvelous providence first planted in him those motions of mind so that he could take virtue as the earth takes tillage, and he placed the matter of vices in the affections, of virtue in the vices. Which will surely either be nothing or will not be able to be in use if those things are lacking through which its force either appears or stands.

Let us now see what those same ones who cut vices out by the root have achieved. Those four affections which they think arise from the opinion of goods and evils, by whose uprooting they judge the wise person's mind must be healed — since they understand both that they are planted by nature and that without them nothing can be moved, nothing done — they put certain others in their place and turn. For desire they substitute will, as if it were not much better to desire the good than to will [the evil]; likewise for joy, gladness; for fear, caution. But in that fourth the account of changing the name fails them. And so they have taken away grief entirely — that is, sadness and pain of mind: which can by no means happen. For who can not grieve if pestilence has drained the homeland or an enemy overturned it or a tyrant oppressed it? Can anyone not grieve if he has seen liberty taken away, if neighbors, if friends, if good men have been either banished or most cruelly slaughtered? Unless his mind has grown so numb that every sense has been snatched from him. Wherefore they ought either to have taken away all or this short and weak dispute ought to have been filled out — that is, something also put back for grief, since with the earlier ones so arranged this followed. For as we rejoice in present goods, so we are distressed and grieve at evils. If therefore they gave joy, because they thought it vicious, another name, so it was fitting that another word be assigned to grief, because they think it too vicious. From which it appears they lacked not the thing but the word: by whose lack they wished to take away that whole affection which is even the greatest, against what nature would allow. For I could refute those changes of names at more length and show either that many names were set on the same things for the sake of adorning speech and increasing vocabulary, or at least that those do not differ much among themselves. For desire begins from will and caution arises from fear and joy is nothing else than gladness made public. But let us suppose, as they themselves wish, that they are different. Surely therefore they will say desire is a persevering and perpetual will, but joy gladness lifting itself insolently, and fear excessive caution exceeding measure. So it happens that they do not take away the things they judge must be taken away, but temper them, since indeed they only change the names, the things themselves remain. Therefore they roll back unawares to where the Peripatetics arrive by reason, that since vices cannot be taken away they must be tempered in the middle. They err therefore, because they do not achieve what they want, and by a long and rough circuit return to the same road.
